name: Windsor
lede: Windsor is a deep aubergine-purple in Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary; the books read do not explain the name.

sections.title: A name without a story
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul record Windsor as a dark purple first used in 1924, but none of the books we hold says why it is called that [1]. The same dictionary has Windsor Tan, a brown, so the place name was used for more than one color [1]. Origin undocumented, and it is unrelated to [[romanesque]], its nearest dark purple [1].

Paterson says phthalocyanine blue, first found at ICI in 1928 by accident, is also sold as Windsor or Winsor blue, the latter a Winsor and Newton trade name [2]. That is a [[windsor-blue]] pigment, not this purple.

sections.title: Windsor and the aniline dyes
sections.body: Garfield reports that Hofmann lectured to the royal family at Windsor, and that a secretary wrote to thank him in 1865 and praised the aniline-dyed silks and wools shown there [3]. None of the books connect this to the name, so it is not an origin for this color [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This dark purple is uncommon in paintings: 75 of 23,781, rarer than 53 per cent of named colors [4]. It is most often a hidden color within the painting, in 59 per cent of the 41 paintings where it is measurable [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 8 paintings, 1.9 times the museums' baseline [4]. Its nearest named color is [[aubergine]], 12.9 units away, a loose match [1]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test. [4]

openers: Windsor purple has no recorded origin; Windsor blue is a trade name for a different color.
